newsitem.title: USA: NCAA BASKETBALL-ARIZONA'S SIMON HAS DEAN SMITH REJECTION LETTER ON WALL.
newsitem.headline: NCAA BASKETBALL-ARIZONA'S SIMON HAS DEAN SMITH REJECTION LETTER ON WALL.

text.p: North Carolina coach Dean Smith, the all-time coaching wins leader, draws such respect that even a player he rejected keeps the letter on his bedroom wall as a fond souvenir.

Arizona Wildcats shooting guard and team leader Miles Simon grew up wanting to play for Smith and Carolina. Instead, he will play against them in the opening semifinal of the NCAA Final Four tournament Saturday night.
The Tar Heels were overloaded at his "two guard" position, Smith wrote Simon in a personal note.

"It just told me that he wished me the best in my college career, he was sure that it was going to be successful but at that point in time they had Donald Williams and Dante Calabria at the two spot," Simon said Friday.
"And I still have the letter up on my bulletin board in my bedroom right now."

Simon, from Fullerton, California, said: "North Carolina has almost always been my favourite school. I wanted to go there. I was a kid growing up Carolina blue, you know, any time I could buy a hat or shirt or whatever that said North Carolina, I was going to get it.

"And just having something from Dean Smith -- personalized signature. You get a lot of letters from coaches and it has their stamped signature on there. And he wrote a little note on the bottom to me, and it was just something that I can treasure."
Simon said: "It's going to be a great honour to say I played against Dean Smith in the Final Four the year that he broke Adolph Rupp's (wins) record.
Told of Simon's remarks, Smith inquired wryly: "Does that mean Miles isn't going to play hard? He always plays hard.
"I did write him a letter and I seldom do that."

Smith explained: "You just don't want to over-recruit. At least we haven't in our place. He might have been behind Williams or Calabria. But that's nice of Miles Simon and I have great respect for him. And I just wish he were ineligible like he was in November, for one game only."
Simon, Arizona's only returning starter, missed the first 11 games of the season -- including a win over North Carolina -- due to academic ineligibility. He feels it helped him mature.
"Oh, definitely, because I think basketball was definitely first and foremost on my list, and it just got taken away in a matter of just a blink of an eye," said Simon.

"And there was always the thought in the back of my mind, do they really need me or do they want me back, because they were playing so well at the time. But one thing, my teammates just supported me tremendously and I give thanks to them."

"Obviously we needed Miles," said high-scoring forward Michael Dickerson. "Miles was our leader. After he got ineligible, we didn't even know if we could compete. But we did and we came out and played as a team and we all believed in each other. But we're very happy to have Miles back."

"It's tough when you add another person in there," said fast-developing big man A.J. Bramlett, "but Miles is a great player, he's an all-around player, he plays defence, he's a great offensive scorer and he does the little things you need someone to do.
"Once we got Miles in the flow and he started playing great basketball, that made our team more dangerous. Nobody could focus just on Michael Dickerson as our scorer."
Arizona coach Lute Olson got Simon after North Carolina passed, and he shares the player's admiration for Smith.
"When he's referred to as the Michelangelo of coaching, I really think that's a very appropriate term," said Olson.

"And the great thing about it is the humility of the man. I can remember when I was a high school coach attending a clinic and had a chance to say hello afterwards -- with Coach Smith, I think he's friendly and open to everybody, whether you're somebody or whether you're no one.
"And I think that's a real true measure of the man, is the greatness and yet the humility that he shows."
Smith's players joined the chorus.
"He's taught us how to conduct ourselves in public and how to treat people with respect," said Vince Carter.
"It's just he's a great person and somebody to look up to. And we watch what he does and learn from him and he's made us better people."
"Coach Smith has basically been a father to the majority of the guys that are here," added Shammond Williams.
Smith was asked to comment about the time in 1958 he took a black student into an all-white diner and other moves he made to encourage racial integration.
"When you do something you think is right, you don't worry about it or you don't want, quote, credit for it, nor should you get, quote, credit for doing something that's right," said Smith.
How would he like to be remembered?
"That I coached basketball and I cared about the kids and they graduated and they still like me when they're 50."
